files.text:
Waitomo · Aotearoa New Zealand

The roof of the grotto

The lights on a glowworm cave's ceiling are not worms. Each is the larva of a small fly, Arachnocampa luminosa, found only in New Zealand, lying in a slung tube of mucus and silk on the rock. Its tail end holds a light organ, the swollen tips of its excretory tubules, where luciferin burns with oxygen and gives a cold blue-green light. Below the tube the larva lets down dozens of silk threads, each beaded along its length with droplets of sticky mucus, and waits. Midges, mayflies and caddisflies hatch from the stream below, fly up toward what looks like a night sky, and are caught on the lines; the larva hauls the thread in and eats.

A photographer in Waitomo leaves the shutter open for half a minute or more, in a darkness so complete that nothing else registers: only the points themselves, the threads catching their light in the droplets, and the same points again, upside down, in the still water. The rock they hang from never appears.

Bring a torch, and you see what the photograph cannot: wet limestone, close overhead, the threads hanging in front of it like a curtain of glass beads, and a colony that does not like it. The larvae are sensitive to light, blue most of all. Lit, they turn their own light down until it goes out, and when the torch moves on they come back one at a time, each when it is ready, so a patch you have lit fills in slowly and unevenly long after you have looked away. Here the dimming takes a second or two and the return under a minute; in the laboratory a larva of a related species took five to ten minutes to switch off, and longer to recover. That is why the guides ask for no torches and no flash.

In the dark, the colony keeps its own time. Maynard and Merritt, working with the cave-dwelling glowworms of Tasmania, found that these larvae have a daily clock that runs the opposite way to a night insect's: their urge to glow peaks in the daytime outside, though no daylight reaches them, and individuals that can see one another fall into step. Deep in a cave, a whole colony brightens and fades together through the day. The ceiling is at its fullest while the sun is up on the hills above.

# glowworm-grotto A glowworm cave as a dark plate on the page: the long-exposure picture of a Waitomo-style grotto, blue-green points on the ceiling, their beaded threads, and the same points again in the still stream. Bring a torch to it and the warm beam finds wet limestone, the droplets glint, and every larva in the beam goes dark. Move on and they come back slowly and unevenly. Now and then a midge flies up out of the dark, sticks on a snare, struggles, and is hauled in. ```html ``` The `` sets the plate's size at its own ratio, so the whole cave is in view; a 1 px warm-ink edge and a tight shadow set it on the paper. Nothing is written on it. Without JS or WebGL the `` (the picture at rest) is all there is. The baked layers sit beside it: `grotto-base.webp`, `grotto-glow.webp`, `grotto-rock.webp`, `grotto-maps.png`. ## Options | Attribute | Default | | |---|---|---| | `data-beam` | `.17` | The torch's radius, as a share of the plate's longer side. | | `data-lamp` | `1` | The torch's strength, 0 to 2. | | `data-recover` | `45` | Seconds for the last larva in a lit patch to relight. | | `data-prey` | `true` | A catch 15 to 30 s after load while visible, then every 40 to 110 s. | `glowwormGrotto(figure, opts)` returns `destroy()`, which also carries `destroy.torch(x, y, k)` (css px; `k = 0` puts it out), `destroy.prey()`, `destroy.step(dt)` (tests) and `destroy.state`. Events: `glowworm-grotto:catch`. ## How it works The picture was split offline into a near-black rock layer and a light layer (points, silk and their reflection); the colony's diffuse teal haze was removed, and every pixel of light was tied to one larva (silk to the larva above it, a reflection to its larva's mirror image), each with its own threshold. The rock under the light was recovered from the red channel, which the blue-green glow barely reaches. At rest the shader shows the picture unchanged. The torch is a warm spot (about 2700 K) that lights the rock with relief from its own shading and a wet sheen, catches the droplets, and is mirrored in the water. Where it falls a coarse disturbance field rises within a second or two; once it moves on the field ebbs over `data-recover` seconds and each larva relights as the field drops below its own threshold, so a patch fills in unevenly. The midge is drawn in the same shader: a speck and the blur of its wings, lit by the torch and faintly by the colony. It flies up from the stream toward a glowing larva (one of the bright points found in the light layer), sticks a little way down its snare, struggles, and is drawn up to the larva in small tugs (minutes in life; about ten seconds here). ## Cost, accessibility, reduced motion Draws only while the torch moves, the colony recovers or a midge flies, and only on screen. A vertical swipe still scrolls the page (`touch-action: pan-y`); a resting finger is the torch. The plate is focusable: the arrow keys carry the torch, Escape puts it out; a catch is announced in a polite live region. Reduced motion: the torch still lights the rock and darkens the larvae under it, but nothing fades on its own and no midges fly. ## Credits The cave picture was generated with Midjourney for Taste and processed as above (see `assets/credits.json`). Sounds are synthesised (see `sounds.json`).
